title: Spec browser
summary: A `.spec` folder says what the code is meant to do. The app lets you read it.
description:
Code says what a program does, not what it was meant to do. A repository's `.spec` folder holds that: one JSON file per part of the product, all following one schema, next to the pictures they show.

The folders are the outline. An item's id is its path without `.spec/` and `.json`, and a folder's own item is its `index.json`.

stories.want: to read what the product is meant to do, part by part
stories.soThat: I don't have to work it out from the code

stories.want: a record of what was promised, changed and dropped, each with its reason

requirements.text: Every `.json` file in `.spec` is one item. Every other file is an asset.
All items follow one schema, published as `schema/spec.schema.json`. The file is generated from the schema the app reads with, and a test fails when they differ.
A file that can't be read (not JSON, an unknown key, a missing title) is listed as a problem with the reason. The rest of the spec still shows.
A figure that isn't in the folder, a related id that leads nowhere and a requirement id used twice anywhere in the spec are listed as problems.

history.text: A figure that isn't in the folder, a related id that leads nowhere and a requirement id used twice are listed as problems.
history.reason: Requirement ids became unique in the whole spec, not just in their item.

requirements.text: A spec's size doesn't matter. One request finds the folder and one lists its files; their contents are read in batches, by git object id, only for what is being looked at. A spec of up to `spec.read-whole` is read whole.

history.text: The whole folder loads in one request, so moving between items never waits.
history.reason: Reading the whole folder in one request put a ceiling on a spec's size and on how deep it could nest.

requirements.text: The spec can be searched by the words in titles, summaries, descriptions, requirements, user stories and values. A result opens its part with the entry highlighted.

history.text: The outline can be filtered by the words in titles, summaries, descriptions and requirements. A matching requirement opens its item with that requirement highlighted.
history.reason: The filter became a search with an index: results are single entries, ranked, and can be narrowed by kind.

requirements.text: The spec of any branch can be browsed, and links inside it stay on that branch.
A path under an item's code opens that file or folder in the app.

deprecation.reason: Items no longer list code files. A spec says what the product does and isn't tied to any code base, so the format has no field that points into one.

requirements.text: A repository whose default branch has a spec shows a way into it on its overview.
Items nest as deep as the folders do.

history.text: Items can be nested three folders deep. A deeper folder is listed as a problem.
history.reason: The limit of three folders came from reading the folder in one request of fixed depth. Listing the files first removed it.

requirements.text: A repository's menu, a branch without a spec and the list of a spec's problems each offer a prompt for a coding agent to write the spec or improve it. The prompt stands on its own: it includes the schema, the current outline and the problems.
An item that is listed but not read yet shows under its file's name, and is never reported as a problem.
Long lists show `spec.list-page` at a time. Filtering reads the whole spec once and says how far it is.
A file's contents are read once per run of the app, whichever branches it is on, and forgotten on sign-out.

Requirement ids are unique in the whole spec, so a requirement can be referred to by its id alone: `#S15` in `related` finds it in whichever item it is. In a spec too large to read whole, ids are checked among the items read so far.

A requirement, story, value or item that is no longer wanted is kept, with a `deprecation` giving the reason and optionally what replaced it and when. Deprecated means deleted: it no longer holds, and it stays only so that it is known why it went and doesn't come back unnoticed.

history.text: A requirement or item that is no longer wanted is kept, with the status `deprecated` and a `deprecation` giving the reason and optionally what replaced it and when. The status without the record, or the record without the status, is listed as a problem.
history.reason: The format no longer has statuses: the deprecation record alone marks what was dropped.

requirements.text: Deprecated requirements are folded away below the live ones, shown with why they were dropped, and not counted among the requirements. They are still found by the filter.
`spec-llms.txt` at the root of this repository describes the format for coding agents. It is generated from the same text as the agent prompt, and a test fails when it is stale.

A requirement has a version, 1 by default. Its earlier versions are kept in its `history`, oldest first, each with what it said and the reason it was replaced. A version that doesn't match the length of the history, or a history out of order, is listed as a problem.
A requirement with earlier versions shows its version, and unfolds to its history, newest first. The filter finds a requirement by what it used to say and by why it changed.
A reference can name a version of a requirement, as `#S19@1`. A version the requirement hasn't reached leads nowhere.
The format has nothing that points into a code base: no field for files or paths. An item that still has the old `code` list is read without it, and listed as a problem that says to remove it.
The format has no status. What carries a deprecation is deprecated; everything else is the spec. A file that still has statuses is read without them, and listed as a problem that says to remove them.

history.text: A status says where something stands as part of the spec: draft, accepted or deprecated. There is none for what is built. An item or requirement that still says implemented is read as accepted, and listed as a problem that says to change it.
history.reason: Draft and accepted were planning states, which belong where the product is managed. The only thing a spec records about an entry is that it was dropped.

requirements.text: A part can have user stories: who wants what, and optionally why, read as one sentence. A story can name the requirements that make it true, and each leads to its requirement. A name that isn't a requirement in the spec is listed as a problem.

User stories and requirements share one set of ids: an id used by both is listed as a problem. A story is deprecated like a requirement, with its reason, and is found by the filter and reachable by link.
The format has no open questions: what isn't decided is not part of a spec. An item that still has the old `questions` list is read without it, and listed as a problem that says to remove it.
A spec may specify internals, such as an architecture or a data model, as requirements in words. The format still has no field for code references.

A part can define named values, each with a type: color (with an optional dark-mode value), size, time, number, wording, font or list of names. A value that doesn't fit its type makes its file unreadable, with the reason.
A named value is shown as what it is: a swatch for a color, a bar for a size, a sample for a font, chips for a list. Where text names a value in backticks, what it is shows next to the name.

Values share the one set of ids with user stories and requirements, are found by the filter and reachable by link, show what they were before with the reason for each change, and are deprecated with a reason like requirements.

The format's description, the agent prompt and both handovers tell a coding agent to cite requirement ids in the code and tests it writes, as a comment `Spec:` followed by the ids. The spec itself still names no code.

A requirement shows, on request, the files that cite it: those with a comment `Spec:` followed by its id as an id of its own. They are found by searching the repository's code on its default branch, not stored in the spec. A deprecated requirement that is still cited says so.

deprecation.reason: The spec is read as a thing of its own. Showing where code cites a requirement put the code base into the spec browser.

requirements.text: The spec's first page has an index: every requirement, user story and named value by id, in the order a person reads ids, and everything that was dropped. A dropped part stands for what is in it.

The search covers parts, requirements, user stories and values, and can be narrowed to one kind. The entry whose id was typed comes first, then ids that start with or contain it, then what entries say, then what they used to say and why they changed or were dropped. Enter on an exact id opens it.
A search over everything also shows what was dropped, marked as deprecated, so an idea that was dropped before is seen before it is added again.

A requirement, a user story and a named value can say what else they are related to, as a part can. It is written at one end and shown at both. A story is related to the requirements that make it true. A pointer that leads nowhere is listed as a problem.

The spec's first page offers a prompt for a coding agent to check that the spec agrees with itself: keep the pointers between entries, find what contradicts or is stated twice, fix what has one answer, leave contradictions to a person, and report what it read and found as a careful reading, not a proof. Nothing in the spec records that it was checked.
A user story that is still wanted and names a deprecated requirement as making it true is listed as a problem.

values.description: The largest spec that is read in full up front.
How much of a long list shows before asking for more.

figures.alt: A part in the spec browser, with its requirements, a figure and related parts
figures.caption: A part: its requirements, pictures and what it relates to.
